scenes.headline: Packaging & Distributing Python
scenes.subtitle: From loose scripts to installable packages
scenes.narration: Packaging turns a folder of loose scripts into a versioned, installable artifact that others can pip install and depend on with confidence.

scenes.headline: The modern toolchain
items: pyproject.toml declares metadata, dependencies, and build config
The build tool produces wheels and source distributions
twine or uv uploads the artifacts to PyPI
scenes.narration: Modern packaging centers on a single pyproject.toml file that declares your project's metadata, dependencies, and build backend in one place. The build tool reads that file and produces the distributable artifacts. Finally, a tool like twine or uv uploads those artifacts to PyPI or a private index so others can install them.

scenes.headline: A minimal pyproject.toml
scenes.code:
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "my-etl"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["pandas>=2.0", "pyarrow"]

[project.scripts]
my-etl = "my_etl.cli:main"
scenes.narration: This file has three key sections. The build-system table names the backend that will actually build the package, here hatchling. The project table declares the name, version, and runtime dependencies that pip will install alongside your code. The project.scripts table is a nice touch: it registers a console entry point so that installing the package creates a my-etl command in the user's shell.

scenes.headline: Build to publish
nodes: Get a wheel and an sdist
scenes.narration: The publishing workflow follows a clean sequence. You describe the project once in pyproject.toml, then run python -m build, which generates both a wheel and a source distribution. With those artifacts in hand, twine uploads them to a package index where anyone can pip install your project.

scenes.headline: Wheel vs sdist

columns.title: Wheel (.whl)
points: No build step on the user's machine

columns.title: Source dist (.tar.gz)
points: A portable fallback for any platform

scenes.narration: A wheel is a pre-built package that installs almost instantly because no compilation happens on the user's machine. A source distribution ships the raw source and is built at install time, which is slower but serves as a universal fallback for platforms without a matching wheel. Publishing both means fast installs where a wheel fits and reliable installs everywhere else.

scenes.headline: Best practices
items: Specify dependency ranges, not exact pins, for libraries
Include a README and license so consumers trust the package
scenes.narration: Version your releases with semantic versioning so consumers can tell at a glance whether an upgrade is safe or breaking. For libraries, express dependencies as ranges rather than exact pins, which avoids conflicts when they are installed alongside other packages. And always ship a README and a license in your metadata, because clear documentation and legal terms are what make people willing to depend on your work.

scenes.text: pyproject.toml is the single source of truth — declare, build, and publish from there for a repeatable release.
scenes.narration: Keep all your packaging configuration in pyproject.toml and distribution becomes a repeatable, reliable step. Declare once, build, and publish, and your pipeline code turns into a dependency others can trust.
